doc.title: Larry Gold interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 18, 2025

chapter: The Philly Sound and its makers
title: Gamble and Huff songs: the pulse of the neighborhoods
summary: Gamble's emotional and commercial writing, Thom Bell's songs, and hearing a Muzak version of La-La Means I Love You.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Whoever wrote this promo on your website spoke about them saying, "They also had a brilliant ability to figure out what the people wanted to hear. The result? The sound of Philadelphia." How did they figure out what people wanted to hear?

Well I used to say they had the pulse. They had the beat and pulse of the neighborhoods if that makes sense. In a way it's like jazz. You know they had the beat and pulse of the neighborhoods. So to me that — my phrase that they knew what people wanted to hear, that's what I mean. And also I think if you go back and pick song to song there was a lot of like how do you say this, there was a lot of over—emotional songs that Gamble used to write. He was quite a hell of a lyricist. And some of those songs, "Me and Mrs. Jones," Billy Paul and I mean I can go on and on, but then he had another side to him where it was so commercial like "Love Train." You know that was, it was almost like what do they call those songs candy apple? I don't know the term they use in popular music.
But you know they're teenybops. You know they're like —
Yeah. And Tommy Bell "La—la Means I Love You." You know? I mean just the title alone is enough to make you go oh my God. You know I remember in the early '70s my © Fillius Jazz Archive 10

wife and I were staying in New York one night. And we went into the elevator and there was an arrangement of "La—la Means I Love You." You know? Done by Muzak. And I thought to myself, "Shit this is going to really be big."
